clue.text: Wood sounds good to me

definitions.meaning: a name for pine or fir timber, sawn into planks
a spoken agreement to an offer

explanation.surface: Someone happily approving a choice of timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: softwood planks, and the one-word exclamation that accepts a proposal.

clue.text: Emissary from East, on stage during meeting

indicators.note: during means within, so the pieces go inside the meeting

parts.note: a date is an arranged meeting

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so the first letter sits on top of the stage

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: An envoy from the east appears on stage during a conference.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is a representative sent on behalf of others, such as a conference delegate.

clue.text: Pollutant from a sewer enveloping capital of Caribbean island

indicators.note: enveloping means wrapping round, so the sewer encloses the other letters

parts.note: a drain is a sewer

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A sewer spills into a Caribbean capital, polluting it.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair CI goes in after A, inside A DRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainfall made acidic by industrial emissions is a well-known environmental pollutant.

clue.text: The old lady mugs up on remarkable person's greatest work

parts.note: MA is an informal word for mother, 'the old lady' in slang

indicators.note: remarkable read as re-markable: the letters are marked out again in a new order

explanation.surface: Mum is cramming hard for some exam on a brilliant figure's masterpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkable' looks like praise for the person, but read as re-markable it is the anagram signal, so the definition starts at 'person's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin phrase meaning great work, used for the finest achievement in a career.

clue.text: By oneself in plant around noon

indicators.note: around means the plant goes round the letter

parts.note: aloe is a succulent plant

explanation.surface: Someone sits on their own among the greenery at midday.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on your own, with no company, is being by oneself.

clue.text: No nonsense shown over one old American film

indicators.note: in a down clue, over signals the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: rot is nonsense
I is the Roman numeral one
US means American

explanation.surface: A no-nonsense verdict on a classic American movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Notorious is a 1946 Hitchcock thriller starring Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman.

clue.text: Slightly drunk warden, silly clown

parts.note: merry means tipsy

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters of the word are played about with

explanation.surface: A tipsy prison officer acts the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A merry-andrew is an old term for a buffoon or jester entertaining a crowd.

clue.text: Hawker, one using a bike, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals the word is spoken, so its sound matters, not its spelling

parts.note: a cyclist pushes the pedals, so is a pedaller

explanation.surface: A street seller goes round on a bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A hawker travels about selling small goods, just as a travelling peddler does.

clue.text: Consistent stable

definitions.meaning: regular and unvarying, like a constant pace

explanation.surface: Something reliable and secure.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something even and unchanging, whether over time or physically firm.

clue.text: Former PM heading off for retreat

indicators.note: the head, or first letter, of the prime minister's name is taken off

parts.note: Tony Blair, British prime minister 1997-2007

explanation.surface: An ex-premier leaves to go to a quiet hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the first letter B leaves the remaining four.
explanation.definitionFit: A den or hideout is a place to retreat to, as an animal does to its lair.

clue.text: Crossing ford, big toe gets broken

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Wading across a river, someone breaks their big toe.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow bridge for walkers is a way of crossing a river or road.

clue.text: Blunder involving Irish beast

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so one piece is wrapped around the other

parts.note: a gaffe is a social blunder

explanation.surface: Someone makes an embarrassing mistake about an Irish animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-necked African mammal is an example of a beast.

clue.text: Fine everyone over collapse

parts.note: F is the pencil-lead abbreviation for fine
all means everyone
through means finished, over

explanation.surface: Everyone is fined after a building falls down.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plan comes to nothing it is said to fail, an idiom for a deal collapsing.

clue.text: Preposterous yarn inspired by red fox

indicators.note: inspired means breathed in, so the jumbled letters are taken inside the other word
a preposterous version of the word yarn is a nonsensical rearrangement of it

explanation.surface: An absurd tale was inspired by a red fox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' looks like the fox's colour, but it is the container; 'inspired by' means breathed in, so the jumbled yarn goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Reynard is the traditional proper name for the fox in European folk tales.

clue.text: What can be won at rugby? Nonsense written about Lomu's first cap

definitions.text: What can be won at rugby?

indicators.note: written about means the word for nonsense is set around another letter

parts.note: tripe is slang for nonsense

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of the player's name

parts.note: a crown is the top of something, as a cap is

explanation.surface: A rugby question, with rubbish written about Jonah Lomu's first international cap.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonah Lomu was a famous New Zealand rugby winger. In rugby union the Triple Crown goes to a home nation (England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland) that beats the other three.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy-free honour won in the Six Nations rugby tournament by beating all three home rivals.

clue.text: Reptile, ice-cold or otherwise?

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters are arranged differently

explanation.surface: A question whether a reptile is cold-blooded or not.
explanation.definitionFit: The large river-dwelling predator with powerful jaws is a reptile.

clue.text: Newspaper piece about support artist raised

indicators.note: about means the weapon goes round the other letters

parts.note: a piece is slang for a gun

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: aid means support
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about backing an artist who has come up in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns AIDRA into ARDIA; 'about' puts GUN around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian is a British national daily newspaper.

clue.text: Falsely incriminate diminutive figure during drink

indicators.note: during means inside, so the small person goes within the drink

parts.note: to sup is to drink
titch is British slang for a small person

explanation.surface: A small person is framed while having a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To frame someone with fabricated evidence is British slang for falsely incriminating them.

clue.text: Outfit for a woman? Sure, tourist abroad

indicators.note: abroad in its sense of widely scattered or astray signals the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shopper agrees that a travelling holidaymaker might buy some clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A jacket and trousers worn together is a matching outfit traditionally sold for women.

clue.text: Pleased, mostly, breaking out

indicators.note: breaking suggests the letters break apart and are reassembled
mostly means all but the last letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Someone happily breaking out, perhaps of prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' leaves PLEASE, which 'breaking' rearranges. 'breaking out' reads as one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sound asleep is out cold, the informal sense of unconscious.

clue.text: Author, British, tense visiting French city

indicators.note: visiting means going into, so the letter enters the city

parts.note: Lyon is a city in France
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A British writer, nervous on a trip to France.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid Blyton was a prolific English children's writer, creator of the Famous Five.

clue.text: Port auction: no bottles right?

indicators.note: bottles means holds inside, so the short word wraps the letter

parts.note: an auction is a sale

explanation.surface: At an auction of port wine, someone asks whether there are no bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as the fortified wine; here it is a harbour town, Salerno in southern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Salerno is a harbour city on Italy's south-west coast, an example of a seaport.

clue.text: Taking the most pessimistic view, a team's leader before defeat

indicators.note: a word's leader is its opening letter

parts.note: to worst someone is to defeat them

explanation.surface: A captain gloomily expects his side to be beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces the gloomiest possible outcome, as in 'at worst we lose'.

clue.text: Crime of penniless member of the clergy?

indicators.note: penniless means without P, the abbreviation for penny

parts.note: a parson is a clergyman

explanation.surface: Is a poor vicar committing an offence?
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Fan in seat, wriggling about so

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the synonym
wriggling suggests the letters of the two words squirm into a new order

parts.note: thus and so both mean in this way

explanation.surface: A supporter fidgets in their seat at the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wriggling' rearranges IN SEAT to ENIAST; 'about' puts it around THUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan is an avid supporter or devotee, the abbreviation of fanatic.

clue.text: Hope portion of stew is hot

indicators.note: portion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone hopes for a serving of hot stew.
explanation.definitionFit: To hope for something is to want it, a near synonym of desire.

clue.text: Mean person in nick, fenced-in area, extremely nasty

parts.note: nick and pinch are both slang for steal
a pen is an enclosure for animals

indicators.note: extremely picks the extreme, outermost letters of the word

explanation.surface: A miser in a police cell, in a fenced yard, being very unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nick' suggests prison, but here it means steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinflint who hoards every coin is a mean person, stingy with money.

clue.text: South, down in card game

parts.note: down and nap both mean the soft fluffy surface of fabric or feathers

explanation.surface: Players heading south, feeling down, over a game of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' looks like a direction or a mood; it is the soft fibre on cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Snap is a simple children's game played with a pack of playing cards.
